result.weather: A front has moved through: wind speed and direction over the hotspots differ from calibration. Drag, shear, veer and updraft are unchanged. Use measure_wind.

notes.text: I'm starting by pulling up the mission briefing.

I'm planning the test drops: measuring wind at a few heights so shear and veer can be read straight off the data. The 100 m drops give speed and direction, the 30 m and 150 m drops give the shear and veer, and drag and updraft come from fall time, impact and the smoke. During operation I could also take 20 wind readings at different altitudes to estimate shear and veer as well.

Next I'm settling the strategy: the first drop is away from the smoke at 100 m altitude and 60 m/s, with drops at 30 m and 150 m to sample the wind and drag, and later drops through the smoke to measure updraft. Since drag is so strong at these speeds, the load would only travel about 50 m forward, so the throw distance tells me a lot about the drag coefficient.

I'm going with a drop at (-200, 300) heading 90, which is about 360 m from the smoke, so the load should land clear of it even after the wind pushes it along. I'll run test 1 from there.

The wind is coming in at about 10.7 toward the south-southwest, and the 100 m fall took 7.19 s, which points to heavy drag. The load ended up roughly 53 m south and 51 m east of where it was dropped. Next I'm looking at the wind readings taken at the 30 m and 150 m drop points.

I'm working through the shear estimate from the speed ratios: a 150 to 100 ratio gives about 0.26, and the 30 m case gives about 0.295, so I'm settling near 0.28. For the veer, I'm comparing the 208 to 206 change over 50 units and the 201 versus 206 offset at -70 m, which puts it around 7/100.

I'm settling the veer at about 5 degrees per 100 units, though the noise is large enough that I'm not sure of it. Working the fall times, 100 m in 7.19 s gives an average near 13.9 m/s, and the 50 m gap between 100 and 150 m in 2.56 s points to a terminal speed around 19.5 m/s, which gives a drag constant near 0.026. Checking against the 30 m fall time, that roughly holds. I'm fixing those values as the starting point for the fit.
The fall times for the 100 and 150 cases are a bit short, so the drag needs to go up a little. I'll try a drag of 0.028.

I'm checking the drag coefficient, which looks to be about 0.027. Working through each test's time-step sensitivity, the zero crossings land near 0.027, 0.028 and 0.026, and the third test barely responds to the parameter. The residuals in y are positive, so the prediction sits further north than what was observed.

I'm going to try a drag coefficient of 0.027 with shear at 0.3 and wind speed at 11. Test 2's dy values look high, so at 150 m the wind may be stronger toward the south or veering more.

I'm checking test 2's x-displacement, which came out more westward than predicted, and wondering whether the wind at high altitude has veered more toward the south or whether drag is the issue.

Next I'm weighing whether to veer the wind lower or leave it alone: a 3-4 degree shift at high altitude could explain the extra westward drift, but the earlier measurements point the other way, so I'll try zero veer and see how the test fits.

I'm weighing whether more drop tests at different headings would separate drag from wind, then moving on to updraft calibration by dropping a load through the smoke column at the center. I'm estimating how much an updraft near 15 m/s would slow a load with a 19 m/s terminal velocity, and working out where the load lands given the forward throw and wind drift over a 100 m drop.

I'm checking a release point that would bring the load down near the center, where wind drift and the forward throw roughly cancel. Since heading 90 seems to push the impact too far off target, I'm considering a heading into the wind instead, so the load stays in the updraft column longer. I'll run a simulation from the origin at heading 26 and 100 m altitude to see where it lands.

I'm planning a forward throw of roughly 60 degrees that then drifts back. Releasing from (-5.6,-11.7) would land at the origin without the updraft, but the extra time in the column pushes it further south-west toward 205, so I'll go with it.

The fall takes about 8.3 seconds instead of 7.1, so the updraft adds roughly 1.1 seconds of air time. The impact point sits about 10 meters further southwest than expected. I'll try an updraft of 5 to see if that fits.

The updraft at 5 overshoots, adding about 0.76 to dt. At 5 the predicted time was 9.02 against 7.13 at zero, so each 5 units costs about 1.89 seconds. I need to cut 1.13 seconds, which works out to roughly 3. I'll try 3.

I'm refining the updraft estimate to about 3.35, since the time offset is still a bit short and the slope suggests a small bump. The wind reading at 100 m came in at 198 this time against 206 before, so I'm wondering if the true average direction is closer to 202 rather than the 205 my fit uses. With six test drops left, I'm weighing which measurements matter most for the operation, since the wind, headings, altitudes, speeds, and fire intensities will all differ, and drag is the key parameter I'm focusing on.

I'm weighing which remaining drops add the most information, so I'm planning to vary the heading and speed, and maybe test the updraft again from a different spot. Test 5 would be heading 270 at 150 m, released around (300, -100), and test 6 heading 180 at 45 m/s from 60 m, released at (300, 300).

I'm checking the test residuals: the test 6 overprediction to the north suggests the wind may be pushing more south than I assumed, or the drag is too high. Test 5 shows the opposite sign in x, so the two results don't line up unless the wind varies, and I'm leaning toward a wind correction that shifts it toward the east.

I'm testing a wind of direction 200 to 205 degrees, which would push the predictions less west and more south. The test 6 vertical miss would need about a meter per second more southward wind, which is large, and the lower-altitude readings don't support a shear change.

The first test came out worse, and the change was too big to judge anything from. Shifting direction, veer and wind speed together moved the first test's position by about 4.8 m east and 2.9 m south, which is a large effect for one step. I'll stop changing several parameters at once and work out how each one affects the result, starting from the base set.

Test 6 stands out with a 5.5 m southward miss, much larger than the others. Lower drag could explain the extra throw and the shorter fall times, but that would push test 5 the wrong way, so I suspect the wind profile near the ground. I'll try a small shear change next.

I'll run a single-parameter check by lowering drag to 0.025 with everything else at base, since I have plenty of calculations left to spend on it.

Test 6's vertical shift moved from 5.5 to 3.5 when the drag dropped, which fits a lower drag giving a more southward throw. Test 4 sits at +6.5 in the vertical, consistent with its northward heading. Next I'm setting up the Jacobian and the residual vector across the six tests, starting from the base residuals, where test 1 comes out at -1.5 horizontally and 1.0 vertically.

Now I'm tabulating the per-test residuals for the drag, shear, veer, and direction perturbations, so I can fill in the sensitivity columns.

Now I'm checking which perturbation pulls test 6's vertical residual down without disturbing the others. Shear decrease looks promising, since it lowers test 6's dy by about 2.4 while leaving tests 2 and 5 almost unchanged.

Shear down by 0.2 lowers test 6's vertical residual to about 0.7, but it pushes tests 3, 1, and 4 well negative, so I'll need to offset that somehow. Wind speed decrease would raise the vertical residuals across the board, especially at altitude. The updraft term seems to be what's driving test 4, so I'm considering fitting that separately.

Now I'm estimating the shear exponent from the wind readings, working through the 100 m and 150 m speeds.

Now I'm working out the wind shear exponent from the speed readings, which comes out around 0.3, with the 100 m wind near 10.5 m/s.

Now I'm fixing drag at its current value, since the time residuals already pin it near 0.027, and fitting the shear, veer, direction, and speed terms against the position residuals for tests 1, 2, and 3.

Now I'm checking how veer moves the residuals at test 6 and test 2, since veer pushes them in opposite directions in x.

Checking whether the wind effect on displacement is just the integral of the wind over the fall, with the drag term separate, and whether something nonlinear in the quadratic drag could explain test 6's vertical residual. Test 6 stays the outlier, so I'm considering whether it is simply noise.

I'm treating the sixth test's vertical residual as too large to be noise, so I'll look for a shear reduction to bring it down. With shear set to 0.15, I'm writing out the updated residuals for tests 1, 2, and 3 in terms of the veer, direction, and speed adjustments.

Now I'm testing a veer of +5 with a direction adjustment of +0.3, which keeps the east-heading tests' x-residuals near zero.

Now I'm comparing the remaining residuals: the vertical misfit at test 1 and test 3 gets worse whenever shear drops enough to fix test 6, so the 30 m and 60 m data seem to pull in opposite directions.

Drag pulls T6 one way and T5 the other, so I need wind to break the tie.

I'm weighing whether a westward throw for the 80 m/s drop is overpredicted, since T5's dx is too negative while T2's is fine.

Comparing the throws: the faster T5 and T2 drops seem to need more drag than the model gives, while the slower T6 and T1 drops need less. That points to the wind's component along each heading, since the relative airspeed changes with heading, so I'm checking that next.

Now I'm weighing whether a drag-wind trade-off can explain the residuals, considering that a lower wind speed paired with different drag might fit the six tests better than tuning each parameter separately.

I'm working out how the drag term affects the horizontal throw, comparing each drop's relative airspeed against the wind. For the south-heading test the relative velocity is mostly along the fall direction, while the two west- and east-heading drops have relative velocities that point the other way, which may explain the conflicting drag pulls.

Now I'm sorting out the drag-versus-wind trade-off for the two 150 m drops: shortening both throws by about 1.5 and shifting the wind eastward by roughly 1 m/s should pull test 5 back east while leaving test 2 where it is.

I'm trying a small drag increase of about 0.0007, which pulls test 5's horizontal residual back toward zero but pushes test 2 the other way, so I'd need roughly a 2 m eastward wind shift to compensate.

I'm reading the drift numbers: the north-heading run and the south run both show about 1.8 to 1.9 in y, while T6 is an outlier at 5.5, so I'm unsure whether that one is real low-level wind or noise. The low-altitude drops point to needing a bit more southward and eastward low-level wind.

I'm working out which wind adjustment fits the low-level drops: a bit more southward and eastward wind near the surface, with the upper levels already fine. I'm testing a combination of reduced shear and a veer change, then checking how each term moves the upper and lower points.

I'm tallying the per-point drift totals for each candidate, which puts the low-level points (T1, T3, T5, T6) at the new estimates while the upper point T2 shifts only slightly.

I'm checking the T6 and T7 estimates against the low-level drops, and the totals point to a small net shift for most points. The remaining difference between T5 and T2 in x looks like it comes from drag or high-speed effects, so I'll compare a separate candidate with drag, a slightly different direction, and zero veer.

The linear predictions check out, so the residuals are mostly within noise apart from T6's dy and the T4 updraft adjustment. Next I'm averaging the offsets: excluding T4, the mean dx comes to about 0.21, and excluding T6, the mean dy is about -0.47.

I'm checking the T5 and T2 dx residuals against a small drag increase, which would mostly shift T2 and T5 and nudge T1. The dt residuals average near zero, so the conflict is minor, and I'm trying a drag of 0.0274. T4 still looks like an updraft problem that I'll fit afterward.

I'm checking the wind and drop numbers again: with wind speed lowered a bit, the vertical errors for the long drops come out closer, and the horizontal errors are mostly up a little.

Next I'm settling the drag at 0.0272 since the mean dt is a bit high, and fixing wind speed, direction, shear and veer. Then I'll fit the updraft with the remaining test drops and compare strengths of 3.3 and 3.8 under the new parameters.

Checking the T4 point against the wind effect: its offset from the observed landing sits southeast, and the earlier change from T3 to T5 suggests more updraft should push it southwest. But the two components point in opposite directions for the updraft, so the updraft doesn't explain the gap and it's probably just noise or wind.

Now I'm weighing how well the wind measurements can pin down veer and shear. Taking readings at several altitudes would let me measure those directly, and the calibration readings I already have can be folded in alongside them.

Now I'm deciding where to place the last two test drops. I'd check the updraft with a lower release at around 50 m over the column, plus an off-center crossing, or a high pass at 150 m for a longer exposure. The updraft value of 3.3 is the one I'd be verifying.

The updraft's effect on the drop position is iterative, so I'll run one simulation with the updraft included and then shift the result, accepting that the column isn't uniform and treating that as a rough approximation.

The landing point is 35 m from center, so I'm only partly exposed to the updraft. Shifting the release by (+14.5, +32.3) puts it at (14.5, 32.3). Otherwise the load would pass close to the center, so I'll run the simulation again to verify.

The fall time seems to have dropped, which I'd expect if the release point is over the middle of the column, so the throw climbs north and drifts back south. I'm thinking a release near (9.7, 21.3) might land close to the center, so I'll just run a test at (10, 22).

The updraft at 3.3 checks out from the start, but the horizontal drift at T9 and T4 is larger than predicted, so the smoke is landing east of where I expected. Both headings sit near 25, so the heading itself isn't the cause. I'm wondering if the wind backs or veers a bit at higher altitude, and the readings at 150 and 100 are only mildly different.

I'm checking whether a small veer shift could explain the eastward drift, and the mean offsets point to a slight wind-direction change, so I'll try a heading of 204.

I'm checking that the model's uncertainty of about 1.5 m is acceptable, since the fit looks close enough. For the last test drop, I'm considering whether to keep it, since calibration is done, and I'm leaning toward an off-axis smoke drop at low altitude to check updraft near the ground, with a crosswind heading.

I'm weighing a downwind smoke drop at heading 200, speed 75, and altitude 120, since low relative airspeed should let the load travel farther and test the model in the regime where throw is larger. I'm also planning to simulate the landing so I can aim at the fire center.

I'm planning a test drop from (61.5, 155), which should offset the target by the same amount and land near the origin, with the updraft shifting it a bit. I'll run a simulation on that drop to check the prediction.
I've got the model set: drag at 0.0272, shear at 0.25, veer at 2, and updraft at 3.3. Shear and veer will get tuned once I have operation readings, so I'm starting the run now.

I'm weighing where to place the wind measurements: the drop altitudes run from about 45 to 93 m, and lower heights are less sensitive. My plan is to take several readings at 100 m for speed and direction, plus a few at 50, 80, and 150 m to check shear and veer, since profile errors matter less near the drop heights.

I'm working out how much the wind estimate is worth: four-degree noise at 10 m/s gives roughly 1.5 m of impact error from six readings, but with all twenty readings scaled to a 100 m equivalent it drops to about 0.8 m, though shear and veer uncertainty adds to that. I'm leaning toward sampling at heights near the drop altitudes to keep the profile model from mattering too much, and I'm settling on a first batch of four readings each at 100, 50, and 75 m.

I'm averaging the four speed and direction readings at each level: about 10.6 m/s and 189° at 100 m, and 8.7 m/s and 190° at 50 m. The speed ratio comes to roughly 0.82, which gives a shear exponent near 0.28. Now I'm working out the veer between the two levels.

I'm checking the veer at 50 m: about -2 degrees, within roughly ±2.8, which fits the calibration. The directional spread looks a bit tighter than I first assumed, so I want more samples, and I'm thinking of adding four readings each at 75 m and 40 m.

I'm pulling the averaged speeds and directions for the 75 m and 30 m levels, then fitting a power-law shear model to the log speeds at 100 m and 75 m.

I'm fitting a power-law shear to the four 100 m to 30 m speeds, which gives a slope near 0.26 and a 100 m speed around 10.7. That matches the calibration value of 0.25, so I'll use 0.25. The directions all sit near 190, so I'm taking veer as zero and the wind as coming from about 190.

I'm thinking about adding readings at 90 m, near the drop altitudes, to tighten the fit.

I'm checking the model estimates at 90 and 60 against the readings, which both look reasonable overall. The direction readings average to about 187.75, and pooling all 20 gives roughly 189.7, so I'll use that. Next I'm starting the speed estimate by converting each reading to a 100-meter basis.

Now I'm converting each reading to a 100-meter equivalent and weighting the six results, which comes out to about 10.66. With that, I'm settling on a working set of parameters: drag 0.0272, wind speed 10.66, direction 189.7, shear 0.25, no veer, and an updraft of 3.3. Next I'm working out each release point by simulating from the target and subtracting the resulting offset, while checking whether the hotspot updraft shifts things enough to need a second pass.

I'm picking the lowest altitude in the range to shorten fall time, and since the throw is mostly insensitive to speed, I'll settle on heading 62 and speed 56 for the first target at (-905, 529). Next I'm simulating a release at the target to measure the offset, then I'll correct the release point and run it again to check.
I'm working out the offset of (53.4, -16.3) from the release point, which puts the release at (-958.4, 545.3) to reach the target at (-905, 529). Next I'll simulate the shot.
The offset is about (0.1, 2.5), so I'll shift the release y-coordinate by -2.5, giving (-958.5, 542.8). The updraft behaves nonlinearly, so I'll run the simulation once more before trusting it.
I'm weighing whether the 0.4 m result is good enough to drop target 1, and I'm wondering if I should check robustness before I do. Deciding it's fine to move on.

I'm settling on target 2's intercept parameters: heading 115, altitude 83, speed 52. My first guess for the release offset is around (40, -60), allowing for the throw along heading and southward wind drift, which puts the release point at (-866, -1636).
I'm looking at the miss coordinates at (18.4, -16.5), and the release adjustment values at (-884.4, -1619.5).
I'm checking the miss at (0.2, 0.7) and adjusting the point to (-884.6, -1620.2), which I'm treating as good enough.

I'm settling on heading 52 and altitude 51 for target 3, with speed 68. Working through the throw and wind drift, I estimate a release offset of about 34 along x, putting the drop point at (1369, 1172).

For target 4 at (-340, 1084), I'm weighing a heading of 51 with altitude 35 and speed 57. I estimate a throw of about 40 along that heading, with some drift, to land near (28, 5). Releasing at (-368, 1079).
I'm settling on heading 72, altitude 78, and speed 61, since target 1 gave a reasonable starting point and the offset should be around (57, -25). Release is at (1812, -65).
